name: Starship and Mars
short_status: SpaceX has never launched anything to Mars. Starship flew thirteen tests without reaching orbit before Flight 14 reached it on 28 September 2026, and as of that date SpaceX's own website offers cargo to the Martian surface no earlier than 2028.
tagline: SpaceX · United States · Programme · 2016 · Announced In development
stats: Starship flight to reach orbit in fourteen integrated tests since April 2023: Flight 14, on 28 September 2026
earliest date SpaceX's own website now gives for cargo flights to the Martian surface
per metric ton, the advertised price of Starship cargo to Mars

facts.label: What SpaceX itself currently offers
facts.value: The Mars Missions panel on SpaceX's own Mars page reads: 'Starship cargo flights to the Martian surface for research, development, and exploratory missions start no earlier than 2028, at a rate of $100 million per metric ton.' It then invites enquiries about payload masses, pricing and timeframes to sales@spacex.com. The identical sentence appears on the Moon page with 'lunar surface' substituted, and the same 2028 date and price. We read this text directly out of the page data that spacex.com serves, because the page is a client-rendered application that returns no text to a fetcher and its Wayback captures are empty. ScienceBlog reported the same wording, with the same date and the same price, on 15 August 2026.

facts.label: What else that page says
facts.value: The page is headed 'Mars & Beyond' with the subheading 'THE ROAD TO MAKING HUMANITY MULTIPLANETARY'. Its 'A City on Mars' panel states that a self-sufficient city will require upwards of one million people and millions of tonnes of cargo, delivered by 'launching more than 10 times per day to maximize transfer windows that open up every approximately 26 months', with 'several thousand Starships' ultimately involved. Its 'Landing on Mars' panel states that Starship will enter the Martian atmosphere at 7.5 km/s and decelerate aerodynamically, and that higher levels of atomic oxygen are expected to make entry harsher than at Earth. Unlike the pricing sentence, this panel text has no second source: it was last read out of the same page data on 28 September 2026 and cannot be checked by opening the link.

facts.label: The vehicle, in SpaceX's own numbers
facts.value: 124 metres tall, 9 metres in diameter, designed to carry more than 100 metric tonnes to orbit in a fully reusable configuration, with a Super Heavy booster and a Starship upper stage both built from stainless steel and burning methane and oxygen. Methane was chosen partly because it can in principle be synthesised on Mars from atmospheric carbon dioxide and water ice.

facts.label: Flight record
facts.value: Thirteen integrated flight tests from April 2023 to July 2026, none of which reached orbit; Flight 14, on 28 September 2026, was the first that did. Flight 12 on 22 May 2026 was the debut of the Block 3 or V3 vehicle and the first use of the second Starbase pad; its booster relit only 20 of the 33 engines intended for the boostback burn, aborted it, and hit the water hard when only one engine lit for landing, while the ship reached its planned cutoff, deployed 20 mass simulators and two modified Starlink satellites, and flew a nominal reentry and landing flip. Flight 13 on 24 July 2026 deployed 20 Starlink V3 satellites on a suborbital trajectory, so they reentered with the ship.

facts.label: The ship that floated
facts.value: Flight 13's upper stage survived splashdown and tipping over in the Indian Ocean instead of exploding, which had never happened before. After about 24 days at sea, SpaceX announced on 18 August 2026 that its recovery team had brought it to calmer water off Christmas Island, and on 27 August the company said it had been loaded onto a semi-submersible ship for a voyage of several months back to Starbase. At the company's 4 August 2026 earnings call Elon Musk said of the heat shield: 'I think we consider the heat shield problem solved at this point.'

facts.label: The two prerequisites
facts.value: Orbit and orbital propellant transfer. Flight 14 was billed as Starship's first attempt at low Earth orbit; announced on 4 August 2026 for the end of that month, it slipped into September, and on 20 August Musk said SpaceX would 'probably catch the ship with the tower in a few months', dropping the catch from that flight. It reached orbit on 28 September 2026. Propellant transfer between two vehicles has not been demonstrated. Gwynne Shotwell on 4 August 2026: 'propellant transfer in orbit is critical to both our internal SpaceX as well as our HLS ambitions.'

facts.label: Why refuelling is the gate
facts.value: A Starship that reaches low Earth orbit has spent almost all its propellant getting there. Every Mars architecture SpaceX has published since 2016 depends on filling it up again in orbit from tanker Starships before it departs. In May 2025 Musk put the odds of making the 2026 window at 'a 50/50 chance', naming refuelling in orbit as the biggest hurdle.

facts.label: The date history
facts.value: In April 2016 SpaceX said it would land an uncrewed Red Dragon on Mars as early as 2018. In September 2017 the first two cargo missions were targeted at the 2022 window, a date Musk said was 'not a typo'. On 7 September 2024 he said the first uncrewed Starships would leave in the 2026 window and, if those landings went well, 'the first crewed flights to Mars will be in 4 years', that is about 2028. In May 2025 he gave the 2026 window a 50 per cent chance. SpaceX's website now says no earlier than 2028. The architecture changed completely at least once along the way, so these dates do not all belong to one vehicle.

facts.label: Red Dragon
facts.value: The 2016 plan was a modified Dragon 2 capsule launched on a Falcon Heavy and landing propulsively on its SuperDraco thrusters, with NASA supplying technical support under an unfunded Space Act Agreement in exchange for entry, descent and landing data. It was cancelled in 2017 when SpaceX abandoned propulsive landing for Crew Dragon and redirected its Mars work to the much larger vehicle that became Starship. No Red Dragon was built for flight.

facts.label: The 2026 window, and who is using it
facts.value: The published table of Mars transfer opportunities gives this one as November to December 2026. SpaceX will not use it. SpaceNews reported on 9 February 2026, relaying a Wall Street Journal story of 6 February that we did not read directly, that the company had abandoned a 2026 Mars mission in favour of an uncrewed lunar landing demonstration as soon as March 2027, and that Musk confirmed the reprioritisation two days after the newspaper report. The window is not going unused: JAXA's MMX launched on 20 October 2026, a little ahead of the table's dates, and NASA's two ESCAPADE spacecraft, already in a loiter orbit, are to fly past Earth in November 2026 and use its gravity to slingshot toward Mars.

facts.label: The February 2026 reversal, in Musk's words
facts.value: On 8 February 2026 he wrote: 'For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the Moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years.' His reasoning was cadence: 'It is only possible to travel to Mars when the planets align every 26 months (six month trip time), whereas we can launch to the Moon every 10 days (2 day trip time).' He added that SpaceX 'will also strive to build a Mars city and begin doing so in about 5 to 7 years, but the overriding priority is securing the future of civilization and the Moon is faster.'

facts.label: The Mars customers so far
facts.value: On 7 August 2025 Teodoro Valente, president of the Italian Space Agency, announced an agreement to fly Italian experiments on the first commercial Mars flights of Starship. ASI's statement listed a plant growth experiment, a meteorological monitoring station and a radiation sensor, gathering data during the roughly six-month cruise and afterwards on the surface. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell posted: 'Get on board! We are going to Mars! SpaceX is now offering Starship services to the Red Planet.' No launch date has been attached to it. On 21 May 2026 SpaceX announced a second Starship Mars customer: Chun Wang, commander of the private Fram2 Dragon flight, is to fly on Starship's first crewed interplanetary mission, a two-year trip that flies past Mars and returns to Earth without landing. SpaceX gave no date for it either.

facts.label: The Mars launch SpaceX actually has
facts.value: On 16 April 2026 NASA announced it had approved its Rosalind Franklin Support and Augmentation (ROSA) project for implementation and selected a SpaceX Falcon Heavy to launch the European Space Agency's Rosalind Franklin rover from Kennedy Space Center, targeting no earlier than late 2028. The launch is reported to cost $175.7 million. The launcher is a Falcon Heavy, the payload is ESA's, and no Starship is involved. SpaceNews added on 17 April that NASA's fiscal year 2027 budget request contains no funding for ROSA and proposes cancelling it, and that ROSA was already targeted for cancellation in 2026 before Congress restored the money. Asked why the fiscal 2027 request shows no money for the mission, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told House appropriators on 27 April 2026 that the launch funding is coming out of the fiscal 2026 budget; he gave no details for the other items NASA is to supply the mission, such as the radioisotope heater units and the braking engines. The launch contract is real; the project it belongs to is not safe.

facts.label: What is actually funded
facts.value: SpaceX's funded Starship work beyond Earth orbit is all lunar. It won a NASA Human Landing System contract in 2021 for a Starship variant to land astronauts on the Moon, and Shotwell's stated sequence on 4 August 2026 was the Artemis III docking test, then an uncrewed direct-to-lunar cargo mission, then 'boots on the moon in 2028'. We found no government contract, appropriation or milestone payment anywhere for a Starship mission to Mars.

facts.label: The Roadster is not a Mars mission
facts.value: The Tesla Roadster launched on the first Falcon Heavy on 6 February 2018 is frequently described as having been sent to Mars. JPL Horizons records it in a heliocentric orbit with perihelion 0.99 au and aphelion about 1.67 au. Its closest approach to Mars so far was on 7 October 2020 at 0.0495 au, about 7.4 million kilometres, and the next nominal encounter is 22 April 2035 at 0.016 au. It has never been near Mars and was never intended to arrive there.

facts.label: Musk on the Moon, over time
facts.value: The current lunar priority is the third position in nine years. In a July 2017 speech: 'To really get the public real fired up, I think we've got to have a base on the moon.' At that year's International Astronautical Congress he complained: 'It's 2017; we should have a lunar base by now.' In January 2025, responding to a proposal to make Starship propellant from lunar oxygen: 'No, we're going straight to Mars. The Moon is a distraction.' In February 2026 the Moon came first again.

timeline: SpaceX announces Red Dragon, a modified Dragon capsule that would land uncrewed on Mars as early as 2018, with NASA providing technical support under an unfunded agreement.

At the International Astronautical Congress, Musk unveils the Interplanetary Transport System, the design that becomes Starship, and says that if things go to plan people could launch in 2024 and arrive in 2025.

The BFR presentation targets the first two cargo missions at the 2022 window, followed by two cargo and two crew ships in 2024. Musk says 2022 is 'not a typo' while calling it aspirational. Red Dragon is cancelled the same year when propulsive landing is dropped from Crew Dragon.
Starship's first integrated flight test, months after the 2022 window in which the 2017 plan had the first cargo ships leaving for Mars, and a year before the crewed launch promised in 2016.

Musk says the first uncrewed Starships will launch for Mars in the window opening in two years, to test the reliability of landing intact, with the first crewed flights in four years, about 2028, if the landings work.

At Starbase, Musk presents a schedule scaling from about 20 ships in the 2028 to 2029 window to about 500 in 2033, and puts the odds of making the 2026 window at 50-50, with refuelling in orbit the biggest hurdle.

The Italian Space Agency signs an agreement to fly a plant growth experiment, a weather station and a radiation sensor on the first commercial Starship flights to Mars. Gwynne Shotwell: 'Get on board! We are going to Mars!'

A Wall Street Journal report, relayed by SpaceNews, says SpaceX has abandoned a 2026 Mars mission in favour of an uncrewed lunar landing demonstration as soon as March 2027. On 8 February Musk confirms the shift and says a Mars city would begin in about five to seven years.

NASA selects a SpaceX Falcon Heavy to launch ESA's Rosalind Franklin rover no earlier than late 2028, a launch reported at $175.7 million. It is the first Mars launch SpaceX has ever had on the books, and it is not a Starship.

During the countdown for the first Flight 12 attempt, SpaceX announces a private crewed Mars flyby: Chun Wang, commander of the Fram2 Dragon flight, is to fly on Starship's first crewed interplanetary mission, a two-year trip past Mars and back. No date is given.

Flight 12, the debut of the V3 vehicle and of the second Starbase pad. Only 20 of 33 engines relight for the booster's boostback burn and only one for its landing burn, and it hits the water; the ship completes its suborbital profile, deploys 22 payloads and reenters successfully.

Flight 13 deploys 20 Starlink V3 satellites on a suborbital trajectory and the ship survives splashdown intact, floating in the Indian Ocean. About 24 days later SpaceX's recovery team brings it to calmer water off Christmas Island.

At SpaceX's first earnings call as a public company, Musk says Flight 14 will be Starship's first orbital mission and will attempt a tower catch of the ship. By 21 August the ship catch has been deferred to a later flight and the launch has slipped into September.
Flight 14 becomes the first Starship to reach orbit and deploys 26 Starlink satellites.

images.caption: SpaceX's own render of the 2016 Interplanetary Transport System, published by the company on 27 September 2016 with the caption 'Interplanetary Spaceship, arriving Mars'. The nose and upper hull of the vehicle fill the lower left of the frame, its thermal tiles picked out as dark dashes along the flank, with Mars beyond it in the upper right of the frame, lit from the right and its terminator crossing the lower left of the disc.

SpaceX's render of orbital propellant transfer, published on 27 September 2016 with the caption 'An Interplanetary tanker (left) transferring propellant to an Interplanetary Spaceship (right), in Earth orbit'. The two vehicles are mated tail to tail high above a sunlit ocean and cloud, the thin blue limb of the atmosphere and black space at the right of the frame.

SpaceX's own concept art, captioned by the company 'Concept art of sending Dragon to Mars', showing a Dragon capsule marked SPACEX and DRAGON hovering just above a dusty Martian surface with four landing legs extended and its SuperDraco thrusters firing, dust and grit blown outward across the frame.

A photograph of the full Starship stack climbing away from Starbase in south Texas on flight test 11, dated 13 October 2025, seen across water and a low bank of rock and grass, the vehicle already well above a wide bank of grey and dust-coloured exhaust cloud with the engine plume beneath it.
